Nora starts work at “Atelierul Rusu”, an architecture office that restores old buildings in the centre of Cluj. Her colleague, Ana Mureșan, welcomes her, and then the boss, Mr Ionuț Rusu, arrives too.
Good morning! Are you Nora? I’m Ana, your colleague.
Hi, Ana! Yes, that’s me. Pleased to meet you!
Do you speak Romanian? Or do you prefer English?
I speak a little Romanian. I’ve been learning for a year, with an online teacher.
Well done! You speak very well. Look, this is your desk, by the window.
It’s wonderful! And that old building across the street?
That is the Wolphard House. It’s our project. We’ve been working there since Monday.
Good morning, ladies! Ms Lindqvist, welcome!
Good morning, Mr Rusu! Thank you.
Today we study the plans, and tomorrow we go into the building. Do you also draw by hand?
Excuse me, I don’t understand. More slowly, please. What does “de mână” mean?
“De mână” means with a pencil, on paper, not on the computer.
Oh, yes! I draw by hand every day. I love it!
Perfect. Ana, a coffee for Ms Lindqvist, please. The first day is the hardest.
to draw: dumneavoastră desenați (you draw, formal)
to adore: eu ador (I love it)
“ea” is read as a single syllable, like an “e” gliding into “a”: “clădirea”, “cafea”, “ea”.
“oa” is also read as a single syllable: “profesoară”, “oară”, “școală”.
The article “-ul” is pronounced briefly and joined to the word: “biroul” = “bi-ro-ul”, “proiectul” = “pro-iec-tul”.
“h” is pronounced like German “Bach” or Spanish “j”, but softer: “hârtie”, “harta”.
1. The definite article: attached at the end
In Romanian, the definite article (“the”) does not go before the word but is attached to the end. This is one of the most important features of the language.
masculine / neuter ending in a consonant or -u: + -l / -ul
The desk is by the window.
When you say “un birou”, it is any desk. When you say “biroul”, it is a particular, known one: “biroul tău” (your desk), “biroul de lângă fereastră” (the desk by the window).
2. The definite article in the plural
The simple rule: masculine nouns take -i, while feminine and neuter nouns take -le.
Romanian verbs are grouped by the ending of the infinitive (the dictionary form, with “a” in front): -a, -ea, -e, -i, -î. We start with -a verbs. Many of them take the suffix -ez.
In the 3rd person, singular and plural are the same: “el cântă” (he sings), “ei cântă” (they sing). The context shows who is doing it.
You can’t always guess whether a verb takes -ez. Learn each verb with its “eu” form: a lucra – lucrez, a desena – desenez, but a cânta – cânt, a învăța – învăț.
Many -i verbs take the suffix -esc. The most common is “a vorbi” (to speak).
In -esc verbs, “eu” and “ei” have the same form: “eu vorbesc” (I speak), “ei vorbesc” (they speak).
For languages you have two options, both correct: “vorbesc română” (with the name of the language) or “vorbesc românește” (with the adverb in -ește).
I understand French, but I don’t speak it.
How well do you speak? “puțin” (a little), “destul de bine” (quite well), “foarte bine” (very well), “perfect”. And “deloc” means “not at all”: “Nu vorbesc deloc germană.” (I don’t speak any German.)
These phrases will save you in any conversation. Learn them by heart.
How do you say “pencil” in Romanian?
Romanians really appreciate it when a foreigner tries to speak Romanian. Don’t be afraid of making mistakes!
